title: Factcheck: 10 flaws in the Conservative report on ‘cheap power’ - Carbon Brief
gist: A Conservative-backed Onward/Transira Energy report claiming £320bn in savings from scrapping UK net-zero policy actually increases emissions by 524MtCO2 and rests on gas, nuclear, network and system-integration cost assumptions that multiple energy analysts call unrealistic or double-counted.

insights.claim: The Conservative-backed 'alternative policy pathway' (APP), which drops the UK's net-zero target, results in an extra 524 million tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2) being emitted between 2030 and 2050 compared with continuing current net-zero policy — equivalent to the annual emissions of South Africa.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The plan's own modelling contradicts its central sales pitch that cheap gas-heavy power would cut emissions faster — a credibility gap for any investor pricing in a Conservative net-zero rollback.
insights.quote: equivalent to the annual emissions of South Africa
insights.locator: The plan would increase UK emissions

insights.claim: Heat pump and EV uptake is projected to be slower under the APP's cheaper-electricity scenario than under current net-zero policy, because removing subsidies and mandates (the boiler upgrade scheme, the 2030 petrol/diesel car ban) outweighs the effect of lower electricity prices.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Electrification-dependent equipment and charging-infrastructure demand forecasts should not assume a UK policy rollback accelerates adoption — the report's own numbers say the opposite.
insights.locator: The plan would slow electrification

insights.claim: The only sector seeing increased power demand under the APP is data centres, which get prioritised new grid connections, while the extra petrol and diesel spending needed to replace forgone EVs (£65-95bn over two decades, per RenewableUK) is left out of Onward's cost model entirely.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The plan effectively reallocates UK grid and policy priority from household electrification toward AI/data-centre load growth — relevant for anyone modelling UK data-centre power availability or EV-adjacent demand.
insights.quote: APP makes the electricity system cheaper partly by electrifying Britain less – while leaving the fuel costs that replace electricity outside the model.
insights.locator: Daniela Quiroga / Tara Singh LinkedIn reaction

insights.claim: Onward's own modelling shows the UK's gas-to-electricity 'spark gap' would barely narrow under the APP by 2050, undermining its claim that cheaper electricity alone (without subsidies) would be enough to drive consumers to heat pumps.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Bets on a policy-driven UK heat-pump demand surge should not rely on price signals alone materializing under a deregulated pathway.
insights.quote: its own modelling indicates that the gas-electricity price ratio would actually rise in the early years and end up only marginally lower than today by 2050
insights.locator: Matt Elliott, ECIU, on the 'spark gap'

insights.claim: The APP scenario assumes gas prices fall back to pre-conflict levels and stay flat for the next two decades — an assumption Aurora Energy Research calls 'hard to fathom' and out of line with mainstream market forecasts.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Any downstream cost comparison in the report inherits this single fragile assumption — a flat, low gas price is the load-bearing input for the plan's entire 'cheap power' case.
insights.locator: Gas prices are unlikely to remain low and stable

insights.claim: Four years of gas-price shocks from the post-pandemic demand surge and the Russia-Ukraine war already cost the UK £183bn, according to 2025 analysis by E3G and ECIU — a real-world base rate the APP's 'low, stable gas price' assumption disregards.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Historical volatility of this magnitude is the benchmark against which any 'gas prices will stay low' energy-policy scenario should be stress-tested.
insights.locator: Analysis by E3G and ECIU in 2025

insights.claim: Onward's own report concedes the APP scenario is 'more exposed to a future gas price shock' than the current net-zero pathway, and estimates a new spike could add £6bn to fuel costs by 2040.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The report's authors themselves flag the gas-price risk their headline savings figure depends on not materializing.
insights.quote: more exposed to a future gas price shock
insights.locator: The Onward report acknowledges that the new scenario is

insights.claim: Expanding North Sea drilling would not insulate UK consumers from gas volatility, since remaining reserves are small and gas prices are set globally — making the plan, in effect, 'a call to rely on imported gas, with global gas prices' (Johnny Gowdy, Regen).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: North Sea drilling rhetoric should not be read by investors as a genuine UK gas-price hedge — pricing remains globally set regardless of domestic supply source.
insights.quote: a call to rely on imported gas, with global gas prices
insights.locator: Johnny Gowdy, Regen

insights.claim: The report assumes new gas power plants cost just £650/kW to build — less than half the £819-2,054/kW ($1,116-2,800/kW) range cited in a 2025 GridLab report and other recent analyses of US gas plants completing in 2026-27.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: If real gas-plant capex is 2-3x the report's assumption, the APP's claimed cost advantage over renewables shrinks sharply — a key sensitivity for anyone assessing UK gas capacity build-out economics.
insights.locator: The plan assumes gas plants are cheap to build

insights.claim: The APP scenario adds 21 gigawatts (GW) of new gas capacity by 2050 — roughly 20 new plants and a ~70% increase on the UK's current gas fleet — built on top of the understated £650/kW capex assumption.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A large UK gas buildout is embedded in this policy scenario; equipment and turbine suppliers should treat this as a potential future order pipeline even though its cost basis looks understated.
insights.locator: The plan assumes gas plants are cheap to build

insights.claim: Gas turbine costs are rising globally because data-centre buildouts are competing for scarce turbine manufacturing capacity, per the IEA, a supply constraint the report's flat capex assumption does not account for.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: AI-driven data-centre power demand is tightening the global gas-turbine supply chain, a real input-cost pressure on any large national gas buildout plan, including the UK's proposed 21GW addition.
insights.quote: limiting the availability of turbines for near-term deployment elsewhere in the world
insights.locator: The plan assumes gas plants are cheap to build

insights.claim: The APP scenario more than triples UK nuclear capacity to 20GW by 2050 (versus 13.3GW under the net-zero baseline), all financed through the government-backed Regulated Asset Base (RAB) model.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A tripling of nuclear capacity under RAB financing implies a large pipeline of government-backed nuclear contracts — relevant to nuclear developers, EPC contractors and RAB-linked bond investors.
insights.locator: Nuclear faces high costs and delivery challenges

insights.claim: Onward assumes 2040s-built large-scale nuclear will cost £122-138/MWh — at or below Hinkley Point C's existing £138/MWh strike price — despite nuclear costs having escalated massively since the Hinkley deal was struck (Richard Howard, Aurora).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The plan's nuclear cost trajectory runs opposite to the UK's actual nuclear cost history, a red flag for anyone underwriting future UK nuclear project economics on Onward's numbers.
insights.quote: The UK does not have a great track record of managing down the costs of nuclear.
insights.locator: Richard Howard, Aurora, on LinkedIn

insights.claim: Sizewell C — essentially a Hinkley Point C replica that reached final investment decision in 2025 — already carries a higher strike price (£150/MWh for 2039) than Onward's forecast range for cheaper 2040s nuclear, direct real-world evidence against the report's declining-cost assumption.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The most recent comparable UK nuclear project is already pricing above the report's forward assumptions, suggesting Onward's nuclear LCOE range is aspirational rather than evidence-based.
insights.locator: In fact, Sizewell C

insights.claim: Onward's nuclear capex assumption of £10,000-12,500/kW is already undercut by reality: EDF's current Hinkley Point C cost estimate is £10,736/kW nominal, or roughly £14,724/kW once adjusted for 2026 inflation — about £2,500/kW above the report's own 10-years-out figure, today.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Nuclear capex is already running above what the report assumes will be true a decade from now, implying the APP's nuclear-driven savings are overstated.
insights.locator: A footnote in the Transira Energy report

insights.claim: Onward's falling-nuclear-cost narrative depends on full implementation of the 2025 Fingleton regulatory review, but the report only applies that assumption in its alternative (APP) scenario and not in its net-zero comparison case — an inconsistent modelling choice that inflates the apparent gap between the two pathways.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Asymmetric application of a cost-reducing policy assumption across only one of two compared scenarios artificially widens the reported savings gap — a modelling red flag investors should discount for.
insights.locator: In March 2026, the Labour government committed

insights.claim: £137bn of Onward's claimed £320bn total savings comes from an assumed 86% cut in transmission investment (from £137bn to £19bn) versus the net-zero baseline scenario.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Network-cost reduction is the single largest line item in the plan's savings claim, making it the most important assumption to stress-test when evaluating the £320bn headline figure.
insights.locator: The report’s high network cost estimates do not ‘add up’

insights.claim: RenewableUK calls the 86% network-cost cut 'an extraordinarily aggressive assumption,' noting the APP scenario still has to support 32m EVs/hybrids, 6m+ additional heat pumps, 45GW gas, 20GW nuclear and 62TWh/year of data-centre demand on a far smaller grid investment budget.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The demand and generation growth baked into the same scenario appears inconsistent with the shrunken grid-investment figure used to justify its savings — a credibility gap in the plan's core cost model.
insights.quote: rests on an extraordinarily aggressive assumption about how little grid Britain will need
insights.locator: Tara Singh, RenewableUK, on LinkedIn

insights.claim: Aurora's Ashutosh Padelkar identifies apparent double counting: Onward books savings from both a smaller network build-out and lower balancing costs, even though a bigger grid is what typically reduces balancing and constraint costs in the first place.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A methodological double-count this large (network savings plus balancing savings that are causally linked) should materially discount the plan's £320bn headline claim.
insights.quote: we’re paying both to fix the problem and to have the problem
insights.locator: Ashutosh Padelkar, Aurora, on network vs balancing costs

insights.claim: National Energy System Operator (Neso) data shows that with no transmission expansion, constraint costs could reach roughly £12.7bn a year by 2030, while building new network capacity could cut those costs by as much as 75% — directly contradicting the idea that a smaller grid saves money system-wide.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Independent grid-operator data undercuts the report's core logic that under-investing in transmission reduces total system cost.
insights.locator: As noted by the National Energy System Operator (Neso)

insights.claim: Onward's central cost argument rests on a claimed wind/solar 'system integration cost' of £125/MWh — an estimate multiple independent analysts describe as far above generation costs and out of step with mainstream research.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: This single £125/MWh figure underpins the report's case that renewables are more expensive than they appear — if it's overstated, the report's whole cost-comparison framework collapses.
insights.locator: The system integration costs are ‘far out of line with mainstream thinking’

insights.claim: Analysis published in Nature puts system integration costs at around €30/MWh (~£26/MWh) once renewables reach 80% of the electricity mix — roughly a fifth of Onward's £125/MWh figure (Iain Staffell, Imperial College London).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Peer-reviewed literature puts integration costs at a fraction of the report's assumption, suggesting Onward's renewables cost disadvantage is substantially manufactured.
insights.quote: very far out of line with mainstream thinking
insights.locator: Iain Staffell, Imperial College London

insights.claim: Engineering firm Afry estimates the total cost of electricity in a high-renewables system at £55-75/MWh — less than Onward's integration-cost component alone, implying the £125/MWh figure cannot be credible on its own terms.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A single cost component (integration) exceeding an independent estimate of the total system cost is an internal-consistency red flag for the report's economics.
insights.locator: Elsewhere, engineering firm Afry

insights.claim: The £125/MWh integration-cost figure is derived by attributing all additional balancing and transmission costs solely to 60GW of new wind and solar deployed from 2030 onward, ignoring that these costs are shared with existing renewables and nuclear (Callum MacIver, University of Strathclyde/UKERC).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Isolating shared system costs onto only the newest renewable capacity mechanically inflates their apparent cost — a methodology error to flag when the same integration-cost framing appears elsewhere.
insights.quote: is derived by apportioning additional balancing and transmission costs solely to 60GW of new wind and solar deployed from 2030 onwards
insights.locator: Callum MacIver, University of Strathclyde and UKERC

insights.claim: Consultant Adam Bell (Stonehaven) argues the methodology likely overstates system integration costs 'by an order of magnitude' because it wrongly attributes network and balancing costs tied to existing renewables and nuclear entirely to new renewable build.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A roughly 10x overstatement claim from an independent energy-policy consultant is a strong signal that Onward's central renewables cost disadvantage is not robust.
insights.quote: this likely overstates system costs by an order of magnitude
insights.locator: Adam Bell, Stonehaven, on LinkedIn

insights.claim: The APP scenario ends the Contracts for Difference (CfD) scheme for new renewables in 2030 (with all future government energy support going exclusively to nuclear) and terminates Renewables Obligation (RO) payments in 2033, four years earlier than the 2037 date built into existing RO contracts.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: This is a proposed unilateral early termination of existing government-backed renewable energy contracts — a direct policy risk for holders of RO-linked renewable assets.
insights.locator: The proposed changes could undermine investor confidence

insights.claim: Ending RO payments early could force roughly 10GW of existing renewable capacity to shut down after 2033, since it is unclear what happens to that capacity once support is withdrawn (Tom Haddon, Arup).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A ~10GW forced-shutdown risk to existing UK renewable capacity is a concrete tail-risk scenario for asset owners and lenders exposed to RO-era wind and solar contracts.
insights.locator: Tom Haddon, Arup, on Bluesky

insights.claim: Aurora's Padelkar warns that reneging early on RO contracts undermines the credibility needed to attract investors into new RAB-backed nuclear contracts, since the same investor base is unlikely to sign new government-backed deals shortly after seeing existing ones broken.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The plan's own nuclear financing model (RAB) depends on investor trust in UK government contract commitments — trust the plan's renewables policy simultaneously undermines.
insights.locator: Ashutosh Padelkar on investor confidence

insights.claim: £94bn of Onward's claimed savings comes from removing power plants from the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) from 2031, but Iain Staffell notes this is not a real economy-wide saving — it is a transfer, since the same government revenue must be replaced through higher taxes elsewhere or a larger deficit.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Nearly a third of the plan's total claimed savings is an accounting reallocation rather than a genuine reduction in national cost — a major overstatement in the £320bn headline.
insights.quote: it’s just rearranging things on a spreadsheet
insights.locator: Iain Staffell on the UK ETS 'savings'

insights.claim: Scrapping the UK's carbon price on electricity would conflict with the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement's legally binding commitment to maintain a carbon price, according to Adam Berman (Energy UK), a legal and diplomatic risk the report does not address.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The plan's carbon-market rollback could trigger a UK-EU trade dispute and complicate UK electricity interconnector exports — a cross-border regulatory risk beyond the report's domestic cost modelling.
insights.quote: would run contrary to that agreement
insights.locator: Adam Berman, Energy UK

insights.claim: Onward argues the 16 Ofgem-shortlisted long-duration energy storage (LDES) projects would only provide about 5.5 hours of generation (136GWh total) — 'not enough to make it through a winter spell of low wind and sun' — but Aurora's Padelkar says this 'grossly simplifies' how LDES portfolios actually operate.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The report's case for scrapping LDES support rests on a misreading of how storage assets are designed to work together, understating their real system value.
insights.quote: This assumes a rate of discharge that the fleet doesn’t have.
insights.locator: The report ‘grossly simplifies’ long-duration energy storage

insights.claim: Independent analysis by LCP Delta finds that rolling out long-duration energy storage could cut UK energy system costs by more than £24bn between 2030 and 2050 — a benefit the Onward report proposes eliminating by scrapping the LDES cap-and-floor scheme.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The APP scenario forgoes a quantified £24bn cost-saving opportunity by cutting LDES support, a direct offset against its claimed total savings.
insights.locator: Analysis by analytics company LCP Delta
